We'll comply.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>I am rooted in the earth like a river that has carved itself into a canyon, my limbs stretched wide as if to ask the sky to touch me. My bark has weathered the march of seasons, the rings of my core have told me that time is an ever‑present companion, and the leaves that have swayed in countless winds are still, still, green under the canopy of a place that has never known the bite of a chainsaw.

When the strangers with bright yellow vests and steel‑slick tools arrive, their steps stutter over the moss, the bark of my neighbors creaks like old timber. They are strangers in my forest, their purpose as sharp as the edge of an axe. But their motives are clear, and I feel it: a pressure that gathers at the roots that once held me and steadies the air that once whispered through my branches.

I feel a kind of stubbornness, a quivering in the veins of my trunk—a resolve that I have fended off countless eyes of a wandering squirrel, the careless storm that strips leaves, and the patient, patient rain. Yet as the first cut sounds through the brief hush, I feel a hollow, a feeling of being abandoned by air and sky. It is like hearing a song cut at the middle note, a moment of silence that stretches too wide.

There is a brand of fear, too, deep in my roots. Fear that the momentum of this heavy tool will break me in ways I have never imagined, and that my sisters will fall away from the canopy, casting shadows on the forest floor. It is a tremor of helplessness, a pulse of doubt if this is my end.

And I also feel a kind of sadness for the people: my roots, my leaves, the forest were born to be together and to be part of the wild, and I mourn the knowledge that these men were not meant to have me. I am in a state of disbelief—like standing in a room and seeing a wall that have once grown from a seed, an ache because my very existence has become a target.

Then comes a strange, raw determination, a stubbornness that tells me to stand, to hold, to still. I think of all the birds that rested on my branches, of the beetles that crept across my bark, of the wind that carried my leaves. I get quiet. There is a fierce will to preserve the fragments that one should still exist without me. I want to be remembered, to be part of the memory of the forest – a silent witness to the life I helped generate.

But with each swing, the thick wood that had always been a shield for my heart is sliced into shards, prying the merest tinctures of thirst from the core. My feelings balloon, from brave indifference into dread, from desire to maintain to descent into death. I cannot move, my limbs are basaltic but my feelings, a vivid memory of an old world. And then, the final cut, and I am cut: my whisper becomes a crackle and the trees that once made me hold me, the soil that once held me, let their components pass into that oblivion that is inevitable—yet the forest stands, and something that was once less humans and more earth now becomes the seed for new life.
